nodes.label: Charles Taylor
nodes.date_label: Sources of the Self: The Making of the Modern Identity (1989) · The Malaise of Modernity: CBC Massey Lectures (1991) · Multiculturalism and “The Politics of Recognition” (1992) · Multiculturalism: expanded edition with Taylor’s recognition essay (1994) · Modern Social Imaginaries: 2004 bibliographic edition (2004) · A Secular Age (2007) · Cosmic Connections: Poetry in the Age of Disenchantment (2024)
nodes.description: Examines the moral languages through which people understand themselves and their relations with others. In the selected Politics of Recognition passages, identity develops through dialogue rather than solitary self-creation; recognition can support or damage that development. Taylor distinguishes equal human dignity from a demand that every cultural product receive an identical evaluation. Comparative inquiry should remain open to changing its own standards. His later interview on Romantic poetry describes changes in experiences of cosmic order and argues that poetry can disclose forms of meaning without settling their metaphysical truth. These are situated philosophical arguments about modern identity and historical change, with their Western scope and normative commitments made explicit.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Sources of the Self (1989); The Malaise of Modernity (1991); “The Politics of Recognition” (1992; selected 1994 expanded-volume text); Modern Social Imaginaries (copyright 2004); A Secular Age (2007); Cosmic Connections (2024).
nodes.scope_note: The philosophical resources concern dialogical identity, cultural comparison and historically changing moral meanings. Selected essay passages and the complete displayed 2024 interview support the argument claims; the complete monographs remain unread. Amy Gutmann’s editorship and other commentators’ authorship are distinct from Taylor’s essay. No Canadian journalist or other Charles Taylor identity is included.

nodes.label: Peter Brown
nodes.date_label: Augustine of Hippo: A Biography (1967) · The World of Late Antiquity (1971) · The Cult of the Saints (1981) · The Body and Society (1988) · Augustine of Hippo: new edition with epilogue (2000) · The Body and Society: new twentieth-anniversary introduction (2008) · Journeys of the Mind: A Life in History (2023) · “Augustine’s Friendship for Freedom” (2026)
nodes.description: Studies late antiquity through the changing relations between religious commitments and social life. His work ranges from Augustine and holy people to sexual renunciation, wealth and Christian communities. In the 2024 interview, Brown credits anthropology with helping him place beliefs within distinctive societies and the lives of ordinary people. He insists that historical explanation preserve the past’s differences from present concerns. His 2026 discussion of Augustine reconstructs friendship and communal experiments around a figure too often isolated from his contemporaries. The earlier narrative-debate context remains precise: Stone treats The World of Late Antiquity as a portrait of an age rather than straightforward narrative. Selected interviews support these claims; the complete monographs have not been read for this entry.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Augustine of Hippo (1967; new edition with epilogue 2000); The World of Late Antiquity (1971); The Cult of the Saints (1981); The Body and Society (1988; twentieth-anniversary introduction 2008); Journeys of the Mind (2023); “Augustine’s Friendship for Freedom” (interview conducted July 2026, published September 2026).
nodes.scope_note: Late-antique religious, social and cultural history, with biography placed within relations among contemporaries. Complete displayed interviews from 2024 and 2026 support the new relations. Stone’s earlier specifically qualified comparison remains unchanged; it does not make Brown’s books generic examples of narrative. Original books, revised editions and interview conversation/publication dates stay distinct. Peter Hume Brown and other namesakes are excluded.

edges.relationship: Explains identity as dialogically formed, making recognition and misrecognition consequential for human agency.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary printed pp. 25–37, especially 32–37. His historical narrative and normative claims remain his argument; this does not establish an invariant experience or one shared position of all identity historians.

edges.relationship: Requires comparative cultural inquiry to reconsider its own standards rather than predetermine equal evaluations of every cultural product.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary printed pp. 68–73. Equal dignity and openness to cultural value are distinguished from compulsory identical judgments. Taylor’s polemic against subjectivism is not adopted as a neutral description of Foucault, Derrida or multiculturalism as a whole.

edges.relationship: Investigates changing moral meanings through Romantic poetry’s responses to disenchantment and experiences of cosmic order.
edges.evidence_note: Own answers in the complete 2024 interview on historical cosmic orders, epistemic retreat and constitutive language. This is a philosophical resource for intellectual history; the full monograph and cited poets’ works remain unread.

edges.relationship: Brown credits anthropology’s study of particular societies with helping place religious beliefs within ordinary social life.
edges.evidence_note: Incoming resource acknowledgment, own final 2024 answer. This names a disciplinary resource through Brown’s testimony; it is not a collective anthropologists’ endorsement, universal causal claim or invented mentorship.

edges.relationship: Defends the historical past’s integrity and difference from present concerns against misleading contemporary analogies.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2024 answers on the historian’s task, the Roman-decline analogy and historical truth. His normative position remains attributed, without claiming an exhaustive theory of objectivity.

edges.relationship: Reconstructs Augustine through friendship and communal experiments rather than isolating a celebrated religious figure.
edges.evidence_note: Complete primary 2026 interview, opening and questions on changing friendships and monastic life. Biographical contribution is grounded in his specific argument; reported manuscript discoveries and translations were not independently checked.
